content.title: The stampede that jitter could not fix
content.text:
Our product catalogue service, Shelfmark, fronts a Postgres cluster with a Redis cache. Each catalogue page is cached for 300 seconds. For eleven weeks nobody noticed that every five minutes, at seconds :00 through :04, database CPU jumped from 35 to 92 percent. It only became a problem when a marketing push raised traffic threefold and the spike started producing timeouts. This is the write-up of how we diagnosed it and what actually fixed it, since the first two fixes did not.

The alignment came from a deploy. A restart clears local process caches, so after the 06:00 rollout on 3 June every node had an empty cache and warmed the same 2,000 hot keys within the first 300 seconds. Those keys then expired within the same window, refilled together, and stayed phase-locked. Nothing in the system had a reason to desynchronise them: identical TTLs, identical request patterns, and a Redis EXPIRE that counts from the write, so the phase was preserved through every refill. Eleven weeks later the keys were still expiring within four seconds of each other.

The damage scales with request rate times recompute time. A hot key received about 180 requests per second across the fleet. Recompute cost was 220 ms of Postgres time on a cold buffer pool, so the number of requests that arrive during the gap and observe a miss is 180 times 0.22, roughly 40. Every one of those 40 triggers its own recompute, because the miss path did not coordinate. The 40 recomputes contend for the same rows and buffer pool, stretching recompute time to around 600 ms, which admits another 108 requests. The feedback loop saturates only when the database connection pool fills. Summed across the 2,000 aligned keys, we measured 61,000 recomputes in the four seconds following an expiry boundary, against a steady-state rate of 7 per second. That is a 2,000x amplification from a mechanism whose per-key behaviour looks minor in isolation.

The first fix was the standard one: TTL of 300 seconds plus a uniform random offset of 0 to 30 seconds. It reduced the spike by about 40 percent and did not remove it. The reason is that jitter spreads keys apart but does nothing about fan-in within a single key. Each hot key still had 40 concurrent misses at its expiry moment. With 2,000 keys spread across 30 seconds we get 67 key expiries per second, each triggering 40 recomputes, or 2,700 recomputes per second, sustained. We had turned a four-second spike into a 30-second plateau at 60 percent database CPU on every cycle. Jitter is a fix for synchronisation across keys, not for the stampede on any one key, and the second problem was the one that mattered.

The second attempt was a per-key mutex in Redis using SET NX with a 5-second lease: the first missing request recomputes, others wait or serve stale. It works, but it introduced a p99 latency floor of 220 ms on every cache miss for every waiter, and the lease expiry produced a thundering herd of its own whenever the recomputing process died mid-flight, which happened roughly twice a week from OOM kills. We kept it as a safety net but did not want it on the hot path.

What fixed it was probabilistic early expiration, the approach from a 2015 paper on optimal probabilistic cache stampede prevention. Alongside each cached value we store delta, the time the last recompute took, and expiry, its absolute expiry time. On every read, a request recomputes early if the following holds: now minus delta times beta times log(rand()) is greater than or equal to expiry, where rand is uniform on (0, 1] and beta is a tuning parameter we set to 1.0. Since log(rand()) is negative, the subtraction pushes the effective now forward by an exponentially distributed amount whose mean is delta times beta. The probability of early recompute therefore rises smoothly as expiry approaches, and rises faster for values that are expensive to recompute. With delta of 220 ms, a request arriving 1 second before expiry has about a 1.1 percent chance of recomputing; at 200 ms before expiry it is about 40 percent. At 180 requests per second, the expected number of early recomputes in the final second is roughly 2, and the first of them refreshes the value and pushes expiry out 300 seconds, at which point the remaining requests see a fresh entry and the formula goes quiet.

Measured over two weeks: recomputes per expiry cycle for the hottest 2,000 keys fell from 61,000 to 2,300, a 26x reduction, with beta at 1.0. Peak database CPU at the boundary fell from 92 to 41 percent, indistinguishable from steady state. p99 latency on catalogue pages during the window dropped from 840 ms to 95 ms. Raising beta to 2.0 cut recomputes further to 1,900 but wasted 4 percent of cache lifetime on premature refreshes; we stayed at 1.0. The formula costs one floating point log per cache read and two extra fields per entry, 16 bytes. The general lesson is that stampede prevention has to act on fan-in at the single-key level, and the cheapest place to do that is before the miss happens rather than after.

notes: Tests recognition of a quantitative engineering write-up: fan-in arithmetic, why jitter and locking fail, the concrete early-expiration formula, and measured before/after numbers. A correct judge should score this as substantive and note the specific formula and 26x result rather than treating it as a generic caching tips post.
